strengths: Clear problem formulation for an important and underexplored area—agent optimization as a code generation task
Well-designed evaluation framework with five core abstractions that thoughtfully address real challenges (reproducibility, budget enforcement, structured feedback)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 105+ experiments across benchmark, robustness, and case studies with multiple optimizer configurations
Rich interpretability analysis revealing genuine insights about optimizer behavior (prompt modification dominance, entropy decline over phases, task-dependent generalization)
Practical findings about instruction-agent pairing and optimization headroom inversely correlating with agent sophistication
Transparent discussion of limitations rather than overselling contributions
Clear presentation with informative figures and algorithmic clarity
weaknesses: Modest absolute performance improvements (GPQA: 0.60→0.64; MATH: 0.87→0.88) with limited practical significance established
Budget metric incomplete—counts only evaluation calls, not tokens or API costs, undermining fair comparison claim
Poor generalization: improvements on one task harm others (e.g., +5.75% GAIA causes -17.8% SimpleQA), suggesting task-specific rather than robust optimization
Limited statistical rigor: N=3 iterations without significance testing; high variance observed but not thoroughly characterized
Absence of human baselines makes it difficult to contextualize whether performance is respectable
Framework requires per-agent customization (different optimal instruction templates for Pawn vs. Knight), reducing universality
Limited algorithmic novelty—optimizers tested are straightforward LLM-based approaches; primarily a systems contribution
Narrow task coverage (5 tasks) and limited architectural diversity in target agents; small dataset sizes limit generalization assessment
Causality analysis is descriptive rather than explanatory—identifies what changes are made but not why they improve performance
Unresolved reproducibility concerns: external API variability and potential reward hacking not guarded against
Missing ablations on budget sensitivity, significance testing, and comparison to prompt-only optimization baselines

strengths: Well-engineered VERO framework with principled infrastructure design (versioning, budget enforcement, reproducible execution, structured tracing)
Formal problem statement clearly formalizing the agent optimization task with explicit search space and budget constraints
Comprehensive empirical study spanning multiple optimizer configurations, tasks, and model families with detailed interpretability analysis
Thorough investigation of optimizer behavior including semantic tagging of modifications, entropy analysis, and embedding-based clustering of commits
Honest discussion of limitations including incomplete budget definition, missing human baselines, and external API variability
Systematic case study with agents of varying complexity (Pawn vs Knight) showing instruction sensitivity and variance-performance tradeoffs
weaknesses: Weak empirical results: 8-9% improvements on tool-use tasks and ~0% on reasoning tasks (GPQA, MATH) do not strongly validate agent optimization viability or meaningfulness
Incomplete budget definition: Budget B counts only evaluation calls, not optimizer tokens, undermining fair comparison claim—two optimizers with B=8 could differ substantially in actual compute
Missing critical baselines: No comparison to random search, Bayesian optimization, evolutionary algorithms, or human performance limits absolute performance assessment
Small sample sizes with weak statistics: N=3 iterations for main benchmark with no confidence intervals, significance tests, or formal hypothesis testing despite variable results
Poor cross-model transfer: Table 3 shows substantial regressions when optimized agents are evaluated on different models (e.g., Qwen3-4B on GPQA shows -0.07Δ), limiting practical utility
Overstated claims: 'Meaningful optimization' refers to 4-9% gains which are modest; 'limited diversity' claim relies on 50% prompt modifications without evidence that more tool changes would help

Missing experimental ablations: No systematic study of observation function f despite central role; no ablation on budget size, optimizer instructions, or modification types that actually improve performance
Opaque result presentation: Reporting both average best score and maximum best score obscures typical performance; N=3 runs insufficient for statistical reliability
Incomplete reproducibility: External API variability (Wikipedia, web search) introduces uncontrolled noise; no reward-hacking protections; no actual code link provided
Limited failure analysis: Cross-task generalization failures (e.g., +5.75% GAIA / -17.8% SimpleQA) documented but not deeply investigated or explained

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real gap in systematic evaluation of agent optimization as a code generation task
Thoughtfully designed VERO harness with proper versioning, budget enforcement, permission control, structured tracing, and agent scaffold-agnostic architecture
Comprehensive experimental study with 105 experiments across multiple configurations and three complementary studies (benchmark, robustness, case study)
Excellent interpretability analysis including Git-based semantic tagging, entropy analysis showing diminishing returns, and UMAP visualizations of optimization trajectories
Honest and detailed treatment of limitations in Section 6 and Appendix A.4 covering budget definition, sensitivity, human baselines, and API variability
Strong reproducibility commitments with promised code release, extensive appendix details, and clear documentation of experimental setup
Useful infrastructure contribution to the community providing standardized benchmark for future agent optimization research
weaknesses: Underwhelming empirical results: modest improvements on tool-use tasks (2-8%) and essentially zero gains on reasoning tasks (GPQA, MATH) with inadequate explanation of why reasoning resists optimization
Weak baseline target agents (GAIA: 7%, GPQA: 60%) make it unclear whether framework works for reasonably-designed agents or just amplifies weak starting points
Task-dependent success identified but root causes unexplored - limited investigation into why tool-use tasks succeed while reasoning tasks fail despite being framed as fundamental difference
Poor generalization of optimized agents: Table 3 shows modifications often fail on different target models with no principles provided for predicting when generalization succeeds
Statistical rigor issues including small sample sizes (N=3), no significance testing, high variance in results (Figure 3), and no confidence intervals undermining empirical claims
Arbitrary design choices not validated: budget B=8 and B=5 chosen pragmatically not principled, temperature=1.0 universal without justification, no budget ablations performed
Limited search strategy exploration - all optimizers use sequential modification (depth-first search) with no comparison to structured search strategies, limiting insights into optimization potential
Semantic tagging methodology lacks rigor: no inter-rater reliability assessment, category overlap between prompt/workflow changes, substantial 'Other' category suggesting incomplete taxonomy

Insufficient analysis of failures and counterintuitive results: why GPT-5.2 excels on GPQA but fails on GAIA/Retail, what causes -17.78% regression in SimpleQA when optimizing GAIA, why Minimal guidance works opposite for Pawn vs. Knight
No comparison with related work on shared tasks to demonstrate code-based optimization outperforms prompt optimization frameworks like DSPy or TextGrad
Missing human performance baselines for context on whether LLM optimizers approach expert capability, limiting interpretation of achieved improvements
Case study limited to single task (GAIA) with only two agent complexities and single budget, reducing generalizability of findings

strengths: Well-motivated infrastructure design with concrete empirical motivation (A.5 demonstrates real failure modes like test data leakage and budget overruns when controls are absent)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 120 experiments across 5 tasks with proper controls, complemented by robustness studies, case studies, and interpretability analyses
Honest and candid findings: acknowledges that reasoning tasks show near-zero improvement across all budget levels, attributing this to fundamental limitations rather than methodology
Practical infrastructure with five well-designed abstractions (Git Worktree, Dataset, Filesystem, Experiment Database, Evaluator) that are concrete and coding-agent-agnostic
Excellent reproducibility practices: extensive appendices documenting dataset splits, per-iteration results, trajectories, and unrestricted optimization experiment (A.5) to validate design claims
Valuable real-world case study (TerminalBench-2) demonstrating applicability to long-horizon tasks and providing nuanced analysis (bug fixes don't always translate to gains)
Thoughtful semantic analysis of optimization behavior (Figure 4, entropy collapse patterns) revealing that prompt modifications dominate (>50%) and structural changes have low diversity
Appropriate safety and ethical considerations regarding autonomous code evolution with meaningful Impact Statement
weaknesses: Modest and task-dependent gains limit practical impact: 11% average improvement overall, 8-9% on favorable tool-use tasks, essentially zero on reasoning tasks (GPQA/MATH flat across B∈{2,4,8,16,32})
Generalization is brittle: robustness study shows poor cross-model transfer (GAIA gains with Sonnet become negative with Gemini-Flash); cross-task regressions up to -17.8% (Appendix A.3.4)

Evaluation methodology gaps: (1) evaluation stochasticity uncontrolled despite potentially exceeding optimization gains, (2) budget counts invocations not tokens/cost, (3) inconsistent split strategies per task, (4) TerminalBench with N=1 iteration insufficient for strong conclusions

Limited mechanistic understanding of optimization dynamics: why minimal instructions work best for sophisticated agents is counterintuitive but poorly explained; no systematic analysis of which modification types reliably help or hurt

Low semantic diversity suggests fundamental limits: >50% of modifications are prompt-only, entropy collapses after first phase, diff embeddings show clustering of final commits indicating solution convergence rather than diversity
Minimal baseline comparison: only GEPA baseline (0.54 vs VERO Default's 0.61); no comparison with DSPy, TextGrad, or ADAS on identical tasks to assess VERO's advantage beyond infrastructure
Ad-hoc instruction template design with no principled methodology: four templates appear hand-crafted; lack of systematic guidance on constructing effective templates for practitioners

Limited benchmark scope: five relatively homogeneous tasks (QA, tool-use, math), simple target agents (4-6 tools, 25-140 line prompts), all use GPT-4.1 mini; unclear if VERO scales to complex production agents
Concurrent work (Meta-Harness, Lee et al. 2026) converges on nearly identical design choices, diminishing novelty of infrastructure contributions
Missing human baselines and error analysis: difficult to assess gap between human developers and LLM optimizers; no systematic investigation of failure modes or why reasoning tasks don't improve

strengths: Well-engineered infrastructure with clear motivation: Section A.5 empirically demonstrates that prompt-only constraints are insufficient for preventing evaluation contamination and budget overruns, providing strong justification for infrastructure-level controls.

Comprehensive experimental design spanning multiple complementary studies (benchmark, robustness, case studies), reasonable ablations, and thorough interpretability analysis with example trajectories.
Strong focus on reproducibility: dependency locking, deterministic dataset splits, detailed documentation, and version control enable reliable future comparison.

Formal problem statement clearly identifies six concrete requirements (versioning, budget enforcement, permission control, reproducible execution, structured tracing, standardized observation interface).
Honest limitations discussion explicitly acknowledging budget definition incompleteness, missing human baselines, and external API variability.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contributions (Git versioning, budget tracking via gated calls, pattern-based access control) are standard software engineering practices applied to agent optimization, not methodological innovations.

Weak and unsurprising empirical findings: (a) modest 6-8% gains that don't transfer across models; (b) instruction sensitivity is observed but no principled design methodology provided; (c) optimizer preference for prompts is expected given prior work. Failure on reasoning tasks (MATH, GPQA) dismissed as 'a feature not a bug' rather than investigated.

Insufficient baselines and comparisons: Only GEPA compared externally. No comparison to evolutionary methods, hand-crafted modifications, or beam/tree search. Concurrent work (ADAS, AFlow) mentioned but not empirically compared. Meta-Harness convergence noted but not validated.

Incomplete budget accounting: B counts full evaluations, but optimizers differ dramatically in computational cost (4.3M vs. 2.3M tokens in Table 15), making cross-optimizer comparison unfair. No control for inference time.

Weak statistical rigor: N=3 iterations for benchmark study modest given variance; TerminalBench uses N=1 (insufficient); robustness study shows ±8pp variation across model substitutions. GPQA best commits selected on train performance (acknowledged overfitting risk).

Unaddressed fundamental questions: When does agent optimization succeed? Why do instructions matter so much (Table 8: 0.88-6.79% variance)? What makes modifications successful? Can we predict which changes work? No mechanistic insights provided.

Case studies underpowered: GAIA case study 4 iterations with B=5; Appendix A.3.4 documents dramatic cross-task instability (−17.8pp on SimpleQA) but lacks explanation. TerminalBench N=1 with acknowledgment that 'different runs find different fixes' indicates high stochasticity.

Instruction sensitivity underdeveloped: Section 5.3 finding that Minimal > Cookbook+Reasoning for Knight is surprising but unexplained. No ablation isolating template components causing variance. No principled methodology for practitioners to design templates.

Non-standard evaluation splits: GPQA lacks validation split (best commits on train), GAIA uses private test set (validation as holdout), inconsistent practices complicate interpretation. SimpleQA filtered after train/val/test split introduces potential leakage.

Budget ablation plateau analysis superficial: GAIA inverted-U with B=32 regression attributed to 'entropy collapse,' but entropy collapse shown in Figure 10 for all variants—no explanation why it hurts some tasks but not others.

Missing experiments: No human baselines, no budget allocation strategy comparison (single vs. independent sessions), no sensitivity analysis of template design, no gradient-based discrete optimization comparison.

Benchmark limitations: Only 5 tasks with improvements concentrated in tool-use; reasoning tasks show no gains. Transfer across models poor (Table 3: ±8pp variation). Cross-task generalization fails (A.3.4).
Concurrent work not compared: Meta-Harness converged on similar design choices but no empirical comparison of outputs or effectiveness, preventing assessment of relative merit.
Interpretability via GPT-4.1 tagging (Section A.2.5) uncalibrated: No inter-rater agreement study or validation of semantic label quality.

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with compelling demonstration via unrestricted optimization experiment (A.5) showing prompt-only rules fail to prevent test leakage and budget overruns
Comprehensive experimental study: 120+ experiments across benchmark, robustness, and case studies with thoughtful designs (e.g., Pawn vs Knight agents testing expansion vs refinement)
Solid system design: six clear requirements mapping to concrete abstractions (Git Worktree, Dataset, Filesystem, Experiment Database, Evaluator) with well-articulated formal problem statement
Honest empirical findings about limitations: clearly reports ~0% improvement on reasoning tasks (GPQA, MATH), poor cross-model generalization (Table 3), and task-dependent results
Rich interpretability analyses including semantic tagging of modifications (Fig. 4), diff embeddings revealing solution clustering (Fig. 11), and phase-based entropy collapse patterns
Infrastructure release with VERO-AGENT and deterministic dataset splits enabling reproducibility and lowering barriers for future research
Thorough limitations discussion (A.6) acknowledging budget definition incompleteness, missing human baselines, and API variability issues
weaknesses: Severely limited practical improvements undermine significance: ~0% on reasoning tasks (GPQA, MATH) and ~8% on tool-use tasks at best; budget ablation (Fig. 8) confirms not budget-limited, constraining applicability to narrow task class

Poor cross-model generalization: optimizations trained on GPT-4.1 mini frequently regress when applied to other models (Table 3: e.g., -0.08Δ on GAIA with Qwen3, -0.06Δ on Gemini), limiting practical value of learned modifications
Fundamental budget definition flaw: B counts only evaluation calls, not tokens or compute—two optimizers with identical B could differ orders of magnitude in total cost, undermining fair comparison

Evaluation stochasticity not controlled: paper explicitly defers this ('recommend controlling for the latter in future work'), but since B counts evaluations once per commit with LLM sampling variance, results lack confidence intervals and signal-noise distinction

High sensitivity to instruction template selection: optimal template differs by agent sophistication (Fig. 3); templates selected post-hoc; creates unfair comparisons and suggests results are hyperparameter-dependent rather than robust

Missing human baselines: no expert developer optimizations under same constraints, making it impossible to assess whether agents achieve 5% or 50% of human capability and limiting practical significance interpretation

Incomplete cost-benefit analysis: optimization costs $2-3 but evaluation costs $180/pass; unclear when VERO optimization is preferable to scaling base model—a critical practical question never addressed

TerminalBench case study underpowered: N=1 for most runs makes 'different runs find different fixes' claim unreliable and cannot distinguish signal from noise; net-zero pass-rate change masks underlying complexity
